title: DHS Expands 9/11 Response Fee to All H-1B and L-1 Visa Extensions
excerpt: The final rule requires covered employers to pay an additional $4,000 per H-1B extension and $4,500 per L-1 extension, nearly tripling the number of petitions subject to the fee.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has finalized a rule expanding the 9/11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee to cover all H-1B and L-1 extension-of-stay petitions filed by covered employers — not just initial filings and change-of-employer petitions as before.
  • Covered employers — those with more than 50 U.S. employees of whom over 50% hold H-1B or L-1 status — will now pay an additional $4,000 per H-1B extension and $4,500 per L-1 extension on top of existing filing fees.
  • The change expands the fee's reach from roughly 29% of covered-employer petitions to an estimated 89%, nearly doubling projected annual revenue from the fee to fund biometric entry-exit systems.
  • The rule disproportionately affects Indian IT outsourcing firms and large staffing companies that sponsor high volumes of H-1B and L-1 workers.

The Department of Homeland Security has expanded the scope of the 9/11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee, applying it to all H-1B and L-1 extension-of-stay petitions filed by certain large employers. The final rule, published by U.S. Customs and Border Protection, broadens the agency's interpretation of the fee beyond its previous application to only initial filings and change-of-employer petitions, according to immigration law firm Fragomen.

How the Fee Works

The 9/11 Response Fee was created by Congress under Public Law 114-113 to fund biometric entry-exit data systems that track travelers entering and leaving the United States. The fee applies only to "covered employers" — companies with more than 50 employees in the U.S. where more than 50% of those employees hold H-1B or L-1 nonimmigrant status. Such employers must pay an additional $4,000 for each H-1B petition and $4,500 for each L-1 petition.

Previously, this fee was required only when a separate $500 Fraud Prevention and Detection Fee was also due — meaning it applied exclusively to initial grants of H-1B or L-1 status and change-of-employer petitions. Extensions of stay by the same employer were exempt.

What Changed

Under the final rule, CBP has reinterpreted the statutory language to require the 9/11 Response Fee for all extension-of-stay petitions filed by covered employers, regardless of whether the Fraud Fee applies. Only amended petitions that do not include an extension-of-stay request remain exempt.

The practical impact is significant. According to CBP's own analysis, the previous interpretation meant the fee applied to approximately 29% of petitions filed by covered employers. Under the expanded interpretation, the fee is estimated to apply to 89% of such petitions.

CBP projected that H-1B fee collections would increase from $68 million to $129 million annually, while L-1 fee collections would rise from $42 million to roughly $80 million. The additional revenue is earmarked for the biometric entry-exit system, which has identified close to 2,000 imposters and more than 300,000 overstays since 2018, according to CBP.

Who Is Affected

The rule primarily targets large IT outsourcing and consulting firms — including Indian IT services companies — that employ substantial numbers of H-1B and L-1 workers relative to their total U.S. headcount. Companies like Infosys, TCS, Wipro, and Cognizant, as well as large staffing firms, have historically been the primary payers of the 9/11 Response Fee due to their workforce composition.

For a covered employer extending 100 H-1B workers annually, the rule could add $400,000 in additional filing costs per year on top of existing USCIS fees, which have already risen substantially. These costs are typically borne by the sponsoring employer, not the visa holder, though they can influence hiring decisions and willingness to extend workers' status.

"DHS is proposing to significantly change its interpretation regarding when the 9-11 Biometric Fee is required... the significant harm it would cause for certain U.S. employers was contrary to the plain language and intent of the statute."

— American Immigration Lawyers Association

Industry Pushback

The American Immigration Lawyers Association (AILA) has been vocal in opposing the expansion. In comments filed during the rulemaking process, AILA argued that the statute's plain language tied the 9/11 Fee to the Fraud Fee, meaning it was never intended to apply to simple extensions. AILA also warned that the broader application would impose significant costs on U.S. employers who are already facing rising immigration compliance expenses.

The expanded fee arrives at a time when overall H-1B costs have been climbing. USCIS recently increased base filing fees, and Congress has periodically added surcharges to fund various programs. For covered employers, the cumulative cost of filing a single H-1B petition — including the base fee, premium processing, Fraud Fee, ACWIA training fee, and now the expanded 9/11 Fee — can exceed $10,000.

What H-1B Workers Should Know

Individual H-1B and L-1 visa holders are not directly responsible for paying the 9/11 Response Fee — it is an employer obligation. However, rising costs can affect employer willingness to sponsor extensions and may accelerate the trend of companies restructuring operations to reduce their reliance on visa-dependent workers. For Indian IT professionals on H-1B visas, the rule adds to an already challenging landscape of rising fees, stricter scrutiny, and longer processing times.
